title: Computational Propaganda as a Field
description: How researchers define influence operations, the ABC framework and the global industry of cyber troops

concepts.title: From Propaganda to Computational Propaganda
concepts.contentHtml:
The Propaganda and Mis- and Disinformation topics showed you persuasion and falsehood as old human habits. This topic treats their newest form as a research field: who runs covert influence campaigns online, how researchers catch them, and whether they actually change minds. An information operation here means an organised, usually covert, effort by a state or other actor to shape what an audience believes, often by pretending to be someone it is not.

The field got its name at the Oxford Internet Institute. In a 2017 working paper, Samuel Woolley and Philip Howard summarised case studies from Brazil, Canada, China, Germany, Poland, Taiwan, Russia, Ukraine and the United States, gathered by 12 researchers who interviewed 65 experts.1 Their definition is still the standard one. Computational propaganda is the use of algorithms, automation, and human curation to purposefully distribute misleading information over social media networks.2 Notice the three ingredients: code, automation and people. Bots were never the whole story.

Analysts at RAND had already sketched the Russian variety. In July 2016 Christopher Paul and Miriam Matthews called it the "firehose of falsehood", after two distinctive features: high numbers of channels and messages, and a shameless willingness to spread partial truths or outright fictions.3 Their review of psychology research suggested why volume works even when the content is weak. Repetition breeds familiarity, and familiarity breeds acceptance.4

Two distinctions run through everything that follows. Disinformation is false or misleading content spread on purpose; misinformation is falsehood spread without intent to deceive, which is how most people who reshare a planted story behave. And an operation can do harm without saying anything false at all, if it lies about who is speaking. That second idea, deception about identity rather than about facts, became the basis of how platforms police the problem, as the next concept explains.

concepts.title: Actors, Behaviour, Content
concepts.contentHtml:
Suppose a network of fake accounts posts a true news story a thousand times. Is that disinformation? Judging content is slow, contested and politically explosive, while judging whether accounts are what they claim to be is something a platform can do from its own data. In a 2019 working paper for a transatlantic working group on content moderation, Camille François of Graphika split the problem into three vectors, the ABC framework:

  • A for manipulative actors: who is behind a campaign, often a state hiding its hand.
  • B for deceptive behaviour: the techniques that make a few operators look like many, from bot armies to paid engagement and troll farms.
  • C for harmful content: what the posts actually say.

François noted that deceptive behaviour was where industry definitions converged. Its goal, she wrote, is to let a small number of actors have the perceived impact that a greater number would have if the campaign were organic.1

Facebook's version is coordinated inauthentic behaviour (CIB), a policy it began enforcing in 2018; that December its head of cybersecurity policy, Nathaniel Gleicher, recorded a video explaining the term. Meta's current rules define CIB as particularly sophisticated inauthentic behaviour in which false identities are central to the operation and operators use adversarial methods to evade detection.2 When the operators sit in a different country from their audience, Meta calls it foreign interference. The rules are meant to apply regardless of content or ideology: what gets a network removed is the fakery, not the opinion.

The behavioural lens has costs. It cannot touch an authentic citizen who sincerely spreads a planted story, and enforcement is mostly invisible to outsiders. François herself warned that takedowns in this area remained opaque, while the free speech stakes of removing political accounts called for much more scrutiny.3

concepts.title: Bots, Sockpuppets and Hired Hands
concepts.contentHtml:
Influence operations draw on a small set of tools, usually in combination:

  • Bots: accounts run wholly or partly by software, good for volume and for gaming trending lists.
  • Sockpuppets: invented personas run by humans, with names, photos and backstories, built to be believed.
  • Cyborgs: semi-automated accounts where a person steps in when needed.
  • Troll farms and paid commentators: offices of salaried staff working to quotas, the model Russia's Internet Research Agency made famous.

The biggest operation ever measured did not argue with anyone. In 2017 Gary King, Jennifer Pan and Margaret Roberts analysed China's so-called 50c party, long rumoured to employ as many as 2 million people. They estimated that the government fabricates and posts about 448 million social media comments a year.1 Contrary to the popular picture of paid commenters fighting critics, the posts mostly avoided controversy. Their goal was to distract the public and change the subject, with cheerleading for China, the revolutionary history of the Communist Party and other symbols of the regime.

The tools are now an industry. The Oxford team's 2020 global inventory, by Samantha Bradshaw, Hannah Bailey and Philip Howard, found evidence of 81 countries using social media to spread computational propaganda, up from 70 the year before.2 It counted 48 instances of private companies running campaigns for political actors and more than 65 firms offering computational propaganda as a service since 2018. Almost US$60 million had been spent hiring such firms since 2009.3 Platforms fought back: Facebook and Twitter announced the removal of more than 317,000 accounts and pages between January 2019 and December 2020.

Keep the mix in mind. Public debate in 2016 and 2017 was full of "Russian bots", yet the best-documented operations were run by people, and human accounts are the hardest to catch. That gap between the bot story and the human reality will matter when you reach detection in lesson 4.

title: The Internet Research Agency
description: St Petersburg's troll factory: its organisation, its American personas and its fate

concepts.title: Inside the Troll Factory
concepts.contentHtml:
The most studied influence operation of all was run from an office in St Petersburg. Russian journalists got there first. In 2013 Novaya Gazeta published an investigation of the so-called troll factory.1 The fullest public account came on 16 February 2018, when the US Justice Department announced that a grand jury had indicted thirteen Russian nationals and three Russian companies, the Internet Research Agency (IRA) among them, on charges brought by Special Counsel Robert Mueller.

The indictment described a business, not a bunker. According to the Justice Department, the IRA employed hundreds of people, from creators of fictitious personas to technical and administrative support, and was arranged in departments including graphics, search-engine optimisation, IT and finance. In 2014 it set up a "translator project" focused on the US population, and by July 2016 more than 80 employees were assigned to it.2 Two of the defendants allegedly travelled to the United States in 2014 to gather intelligence. To look American, the operators bought space on US servers to run a virtual private network, and used stolen or fictitious American identities and fraudulent bank accounts.

The money came from Yevgeny Prigozhin, through companies including Concord Management and Consulting and Concord Catering. The work was part of a larger operation called Project Lakhta, with components aimed at Russians at home as well as at foreign audiences. For years Prigozhin denied any link and took legal action against journalists who reported one. In February 2023, by then known as the founder of the Wagner mercenary group, he told reporters from Der Spiegel that he had never been just a financier of the IRA: "I invented it, I created it, I ran it for a long time."3

Two points matter for researchers. First, the IRA was an organisation of salaried humans with managers and targets, so its traces look like an office's working routine rather than a botnet's. Second, much of what is known about its internals comes from prosecutors and platforms, sources with their own aims and blind spots.

concepts.title: Playing Both Sides
concepts.contentHtml:
The IRA's American output was built around invented communities. Its most engaged Facebook pages included Being Patriotic, Stop A.I. (All Invaders), Heart of Texas, Blacktivist, United Muslims of America, Army of Jesus, Brown Power, LGBT United and Black Matters. Each spoke as an insider to one identity group, mixing pride with grievance. The aim was less to sell one candidate to everyone than to deepen the anger each group already felt about the others.

The clearest sign is that it worked both sides of the same divide. In May 2016 the Facebook groups Heart of Texas and United Muslims of America organised opposing protests on either side of the same street in Texas, both run from St Petersburg.1 After the election, the Justice Department alleged, the operators staged one New York rally supporting the president-elect and another opposing him on the same day.2 They also recruited and paid real Americans to stage rallies; according to the indictment, those Americans did not know they were dealing with Russians.

On Twitter the division of labour was formalised. Clemson University's Darren Linvill and Patrick Warren analysed tweets from handles Twitter had tied to the agency and found five handle categories: right troll, left troll, news feed, hashtag gamer and fearmonger.

  • Right trolls broadcast nativist, right-leaning populist messages using real conservative hashtags such as #tcot.
  • Left trolls sent socially liberal messages focused above all on racial identity, some mimicking the Black Lives Matter movement.
  • News feeds posed as US local news aggregators, with names like @OnlineMemphis.
  • Hashtag gamers played Twitter word games to build followings.
  • Fearmongers spread fabricated crises, such as a 2015 Thanksgiving hoax about salmonella-contaminated turkeys from Koch Foods.

Within each type accounts behaved consistently, while the types behaved very differently. In this sense, the Internet Research Agency's effort was "industrial": mass produced from interchangeable parts, each class with a specialised function. For researchers that structure is a gift, because specialised account types leave statistical regularities, exactly what the detection methods of lesson 4 exploit.

concepts.title: Caught, Charged, Dissolved
concepts.contentHtml:
The IRA knew when it had been seen. On 13 September 2017, soon after news reports that the Special Counsel was investigating Russian use of social media, one defendant allegedly wrote: "We had a slight crisis here at work: the FBI busted our activity.... So, I got preoccupied with covering tracks together with my colleagues.1"

Being caught did not stop the work. The Oxford analysis prepared for the US Senate, which you will meet in the next lesson, found that the campaigns continued after the 2016 election, with rising engagement and a widening range of issues. IRA posting on Instagram and Facebook increased substantially, with Instagram seeing the greatest growth.2 Some posts even denied being Russian trolls, or complained of political bias when platforms suspended their accounts.

Read the indictment's limits as carefully as its allegations. The Justice Department stated that there was no allegation that any American was a knowing participant, and no allegation that the charged conduct altered the outcome of the 2016 election.3 Those sentences are easy to skip and essential to keep: proving that an operation happened is a different task from proving that it worked, and lesson 5 is devoted to the second.

In February 2021 the FBI announced it was seeking Prigozhin and offered a reward of up to US$250,000 for information leading to his arrest. The organisation's end came from Russian politics instead. Prigozhin had folded the IRA into a media holding called Patriot, founded in 2019.4 During the Wagner mutiny of late June 2023, police raided Patriot's St Petersburg headquarters, and the state media regulator Roskomnadzor blocked its outlets. On 30 June reports said the holding and the troll factory had been shut. The business outlet The Bell reported that the most likely new owner would be the National Media Group of Yury Kovalchuk, a billionaire close to Vladimir Putin. The capability did not vanish with its founder's fall; as lesson 6 shows, later Russian operations were run by firms answering to the Presidential Administration itself.

title: Inside the Senate Data
description: What the platforms handed the US Senate, and what two research teams found in it

concepts.title: What the Platforms Handed Over
concepts.contentHtml:
In the summer of 2017 the major platforms gave the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (SSCI) data on accounts they had linked to the IRA, and the committee asked outside teams to analyse it. One report came from Oxford's Computational Propaganda Project working with the social media analytics firm Graphika: Philip Howard, Bharath Ganesh, Dimitra Liotsiou, John Kelly and Camille François. The other came from a team at the firm New Knowledge, including Renée DiResta and Kris Shaffer, with Jonathan Albright of Columbia University. Together they shaped public understanding of the operation for years.

The first lesson of the reports is about the data itself. Twitter provided data for 3,841 accounts.1 Facebook and Instagram provided far less: 76 Facebook ad accounts, 81 Facebook pages and 133 Instagram accounts, with organic posts from only a small number of pages, nothing from IRA profiles or groups, and English-language activity only. Google supplied its evidence in a non-machine-readable form, as images of ad text and PDFs, so the Oxford team left it out of their main counts.2

That asymmetry matters. Every number in the reports describes what the companies chose to disclose, not the operation's full extent, and outsiders could not check how the companies had identified IRA accounts in the first place. Gregory Eady and colleagues made the same point in 2023 about their own study: because they relied on Twitter's identification of foreign influence accounts, they could not independently validate it.3 This is the standing condition of the field. Platforms hold the ground truth, and outside researchers see it through whatever window the platform opens.

The New Knowledge team scoped its work carefully. Russian interference in 2016, it wrote, took three distinct forms, and it examined only one: a sweeping, sustained social influence operation aimed directly at US citizens, which it quantified from 2014 through 2017.4 Hacking and other channels lay outside the data entirely.

concepts.title: Organic Reach, Not Ads
concepts.contentHtml:
Advertising was the easiest part of the operation to picture: paid, targeted, traceable. Yet the Oxford team concluded that the most far-reaching IRA activity was in organic posting, not advertisements, meaning ordinary posts on pages the agency had grown itself and real users shared onward. Over 30 million users shared the IRA's Facebook and Instagram posts with friends and family between 2015 and 2017, liking, reacting and commenting as they went.1

Engagement was extremely concentrated. Almost all the organic activity came from 81 pages, which produced 67,502 posts, and almost all user engagement went to just 20 of them.2 A handful of identity brands, not thousands of accounts, did the work.

The operation also had a long history and moved across platforms. IRA activities focused on the US began on Twitter in 2013 and quickly grew into a multi-platform strategy involving Facebook, Instagram and YouTube.3 Peaks in posting and advertising tracked the US political calendar, crises and international events. The highest monthly volume of IRA Facebook ads came in April 2017, after the election, the month of the US missile strike in Syria and the release of the tax reform plan.

How large was the audience? A widely cited figure holds that the trolls reached more than 126 million Americans through Facebook alone. Treat such headline numbers with care. "Reached" means content appeared in someone's feed at least once, perhaps scrolled past in a second; it says nothing about whether anyone believed, remembered or acted on it. The gap between reach and effect is the single most important distinction in this field, and when researchers finally measured effects directly, as lesson 5 shows, the picture changed.

concepts.title: Targeting by Identity
concepts.contentHtml:
If the IRA had been a conventional campaign trying to win 2016, you would expect it to pour effort into swing states. The Oxford analysis of its ad targeting found something else: 342 instances in which areas with significant African American populations were targeted, and a pattern the authors judged to have more to do with race than with a state's role in the Electoral College or status as a swing state.1 African Americans in Ferguson, Missouri were targeted for the Black Matters campaign, and those in Baltimore and Oakland for Blacktivist. Texan cities got patriotism and pro-gun politics.

The Oxford report summarised three strategies:

  • Demobilisation: campaigning for African American voters to boycott the election or follow the wrong voting procedures in 2016.2
  • Radicalisation: encouraging extreme right-wing voters to be more confrontational.
  • Pollution: spreading sensationalist, conspiratorial and other junk political news to voters across the spectrum.

After the election the targets shifted, with new effort aimed at persuading Mexican American and Hispanic voters to distrust US institutions, notably through a campaign called Brown Power.

Two cautions keep this from becoming a just-so story. First, targeting is evidence of intent, not impact; the Oxford authors themselves wrote that more research was needed before anyone could say whether the campaigns had an effect in the states they targeted.3 Second, the strategies above are researchers' interpretations of messages, drawn from samples the platforms chose to provide. Read them as well-supported hypotheses about strategy. The obvious next question is the one these reports could not answer with their data: did any of it change what people believed or how they voted?

title: Detecting Coordinated Networks
description: Why bot scores mislead, and how coordination graphs, timing and copied text expose operations

concepts.title: The Trouble with Bot Scores
concepts.contentHtml:
The obvious way to find an influence operation is to look for bots. In 2017 Onur Varol, Emilio Ferrara, Clayton Davis, Filippo Menczer and Alessandro Flammini described a classifier built on more than a thousand features of an account: its friends, tweet content and sentiment, network patterns and activity over time. They estimated that between 9% and 15% of active Twitter accounts were bots.1 The best-known public tool of this kind, Botometer (formerly BotOrNot), became a staple of academic studies counting bots in political debates.

The problem lies in the output. Botometer gives a probability between 0 and 1 rather than a verdict, so each research team must choose a threshold. Published studies picked very different ones: 0.43 in one, 0.76 in another, 0.25 in a third. In 2020 Adrian Rauchfleisch and Jonas Kaiser tested the scores against five datasets of accounts already verified as bots or humans, 4,134 in all, in English and German, over three months. The scores were imprecise, especially outside English, and they shifted over time, so any fixed threshold produced both false negatives and false positives. Most social-science studies using the tool, they concluded, will unknowingly count many humans as bots and vice versa.2

Bot makers also adapt. In 2017 Stefano Cresci and colleagues studied a new generation of social spambots built to mimic people. Neither Twitter, nor human judges, nor the best academic classifiers of the day could reliably detect them.3 Their survey pointed the field towards a different target: the analysis of collective behaviour rather than single accounts.

There is a deeper mismatch. The Internet Research Agency was staffed by hundreds of people, and Linvill and Warren described its Twitter handles as human-operated troll accounts, not computer-run bots. A detector asking "is this account a machine?" is answering the wrong question about a troll farm. The useful question is whether accounts act together in ways that independent people do not.

concepts.title: Coordination Leaves Traces
concepts.contentHtml:
An influence operation has a weakness built into its business model. Someone pays for it and someone else does the work, so the organisers need their staff to hit targets and stay on message. Political scientists call this a principal–agent problem, and in 2022 David Schoch, Franziska Keller, Sebastian Stier and JungHwan Yang argued that it leaves detectable patterns. Employees handed the same content and the same deadlines tend to post the same thing at almost the same time, which genuine users rarely do.

The method turns that into a graph. Treat each account as a node, and join two accounts with an edge whenever they post the same original tweet, or retweet the same tweet, within a short window; the authors' preferred window was one minute. Ordinary users seldom form such links, while campaign accounts form dense clusters. Schoch and colleagues applied this to every campaign in Twitter's public archive of information operations up to February 2021, plus the South Korean secret service's attempt to influence the 2012 national elections, which had escaped Twitter's attention: 46 campaigns in all.1 On average, 74% of each campaign's accounts engaged in this simple co-tweeting and co-retweeting, while the behaviour was negligible among comparison samples of regular users.2 For the IRA, the one-minute rule alone caught more than 80% of the agency's accounts with false positives around 1%.3

The idea generalises. In a paper first posted in 2020, Diogo Pacheco, Filippo Menczer and colleagues proposed an unsupervised method that builds coordination networks from any behavioural trace accounts share: identities, images, hashtag sequences, retweets or timing. They found coordinated networks in contexts from US elections and the Hong Kong protests to the Syrian civil war and cryptocurrency manipulation.4

Coordination is evidence, not proof. Fans live-tweeting a match, activists sharing a petition and newsrooms syndicating a story all co-post. Coordination analysis narrows the haystack; deciding whether a cluster is covert, and whose it is, still needs other evidence.

concepts.title: Clocks and Copy-Paste
concepts.contentHtml:
Two more fingerprints are hard for an office of operators to hide: when they work and what they paste.

Timing. When Meta took down the Chinese operation known as Spamouflage in August 2023, it found clusters of accounts run from different parts of China that behaved like office staff. Each cluster worked to a clear shift pattern, with bursts of activity in the mid-morning and early afternoon, Beijing time, breaks for lunch and supper, and a final burst in the evening.1 Accounts hundreds of miles apart also shared the same proxy infrastructure. A real community is spread across time zones and sleeps irregularly; a workforce clocks in.

Text. The same clusters posted identical content across many platforms, including short "personal" comments using "I" and "we" that hundreds of different accounts repeated word for word. Some comments still carried a number at the front, a sign they had been copied from a numbered list.2 Distinctive headlines with typos, such as "Rummors and truth of COVID-19", made the network easy to follow from site to site. Shared text, images and links let investigators stitch accounts on different platforms into one operation.

Attribution is the last and hardest step, and different investigators rest it on different evidence. Platforms see private signals such as IP addresses and devices; Meta tied Spamouflage to individuals associated with Chinese law enforcement but would not be specific about its technical indicators. Open-source researchers see only public traces. Graphika, which first exposed Spamouflage in 2019, called its own links between the network and a related US indictment low confidence.3 Patient forensics can still go far. Graphika traced Russia's long-running Secondary Infektion operation, built on fake accounts and forged documents, through at least 2,500 pieces of content in seven languages across more than 300 platforms from 2014 into 2020.4 Good attribution states its confidence level, and you should always ask what evidence sits behind a name.

title: Did It Work? The Effects Evidence
description: Panel studies linking feeds to surveys, why measured effects are small, and the case for indirect harms

concepts.title: Linking Feeds to Surveys
concepts.contentHtml:
For years, claims about the IRA's influence rested on reach: posts, shares, impressions. Measuring effect needs something harder, data on what individual people saw joined to data on how their views changed. Two teams managed it by recruiting survey respondents who agreed to link their Twitter accounts.

The first, led by Christopher Bail of Duke University, studied 1,239 Republican and Democratic Twitter users surveyed twice in late 2017, merged with nonpublic Twitter data identifying IRA accounts. Using Bayesian regression tree models to compare those who had interacted with IRA accounts with similar people who had not, the team found no evidence that interaction with IRA accounts substantially impacted six measures of political attitudes and behaviour over a one-month period.1 Interaction was most common among people with strongly like-minded networks, high interest in politics and heavy Twitter use.

The second study went back to 2016 itself. Gregory Eady, Tom Paskhalis, Jan Zilinsky, Richard Bonneau, Jonathan Nagler and Joshua Tucker linked a three-wave YouGov panel of 1,496 Americans, surveyed from April 2016 to the eve of the election, to their actual Twitter timelines. Seventy per cent of respondents saw at least one post from a foreign influence campaign, mostly indirectly, through retweets by ordinary accounts they followed. But exposure was extraordinarily concentrated: only 1% of users accounted for 70% of exposures, and the most exposed were people who strongly identified as Republicans.2 It was also dwarfed by ordinary political content. In the final month respondents saw roughly 4 IRA posts a day, against 106 from national news media and 35 from US politicians.3

The result, published in Nature Communications in January 2023, was a null across the board. The relationship between exposure and voting for Donald Trump was near zero and not statistically significant, and the authors found no meaningful relationship with changes in attitudes or polarisation either.4

concepts.title: Why the Effects Are So Small
concepts.contentHtml:
These null results are not a fluke of two studies. They fit three broader patterns in political communication research.

Concentration. Exposure to dubious content online is lumpy. In a 2019 study in the journal Science, Nir Grinberg, David Lazer and colleagues matched Twitter accounts to voter records for the 2016 election and found that only 1% of users were exposed to 80% of fake news, and 0.1% of users were responsible for sharing 80% of it. Eady's team noticed the parallel: Russian exposure was concentrated much like fake news, whereas the most exposed 1% of respondents accounted for only 24% of exposures to domestic news media.

Preaching to the converted. The people most exposed are the people least likely to move. Eady's heaviest-exposed respondents were highly partisan Republicans who were already likely favourable to Trump.1 Bail's team suggested that Russian trolls might have failed to sow discord because they mostly interacted with those who were already highly polarised.2 An operation tuned for engagement finds the already engaged.

Persuasion is hard. Even legitimate, well-funded campaigns struggle to change votes. Joshua Kalla and David Broockman ran a meta-analysis of 40 field experiments and found an average effect of zero for campaign contact and advertising in general elections; nine new experiments of their own also averaged zero.3 Persuasive effects appeared only in rare circumstances, such as when candidates took unusually unpopular positions and campaigns worked unusually hard to find persuadable voters. If doorstep canvassing by real campaigns rarely moves a general-election vote, a handful of tweets from a fake activist is unlikely to.

The lesson is not that propaganda never works. It is that the bottleneck is the audience's prior commitments, not the supply of messages, a theme that returns when you weigh generative AI in lesson 7.

concepts.title: The Case Against Complacency
concepts.contentHtml:
Null results have limits, and the authors were the first to list them. Eady's team studied only Twitter, only posts rather than images and videos, and only individual attitudes and votes. Their work could not speak to other platforms or other channels, such as the hacking and phishing schemes allegedly designed to surface unfavourable information about opponents at opportune moments. Bail's team stressed that they could not determine whether trolls influenced candidate or media behaviour, or whether IRA accounts influenced the 2016 election itself.1

That gap is where the strongest counter-argument lives. In Cyberwar (2018), Kathleen Hall Jamieson of the University of Pennsylvania drew on published intelligence accounts, indictments, media reports and decades of communication research. Her implicit conclusion, as Alexander Klimburg summarised it in a review for Nature, was that Russian interference very probably had a major role in Trump's surprise win. Her mechanism was indirect: trolls amplified frames that already existed, and the mainstream press, from its uncritical tracking of social media memes to its handling of e-mails hacked from the Democratic National Committee, carried the operation's agenda to everyone else.

The press really did carry IRA messages. Josephine Lukito and colleagues examined US news articles that quoted IRA tweets and found that a majority of the embedded tweets were used as vox populi: quoted for their opinion, as if from ordinary Twitter users, alongside other tweets representing public sentiment.2 Journalism's habit of using tweets as street interviews turned a foreign operation into domestic coverage. On the Breakout Scale you will meet in lesson 6, that jump into mainstream media is exactly what separates a contained operation from a dangerous one.

Finally, there are second-order effects. Eady's team suggested that Russia's campaign may have had its largest effects by convincing Americans that it had succeeded, feeding doubts about the legitimacy of elections.3 The fair summary is contested but clear: direct persuasion through social media looks small, while agenda-setting, hack-and-leak operations and the erosion of trust remain plausible and much harder to measure.

title: Takedowns and the Fight over Data
description: How platforms and governments dismantle operations, who gets caught, and the battle over research access

concepts.title: Anatomy of a Takedown
concepts.contentHtml:
Much of what researchers know about live operations comes from takedowns: a platform removes a network and publishes what it found. Meta's rules describe the routine. When it identifies a network engaged in coordinated inauthentic behaviour, it removes the fake accounts, pages and groups directly involved, and where operators have co-opted authentic communities it may remove the operators while leaving the real users.1 Findings go into periodic adversarial threat reports. Twitter went further for several years, releasing complete datasets of removed state-backed accounts through its Information Operations archive, the data behind much of lesson 4.

The biggest known operation shows what a takedown reveals. In August 2023 Meta announced the removal of 7,704 Facebook accounts, 954 Pages, 15 Groups and 15 Instagram accounts belonging to Spamouflage, which it called the largest known cross-platform covert influence operation in the world, spanning more than 50 other platforms and forums.2 Yet the operation was strikingly ineffective and often failed to reach its targets in Taiwan, the United States, Australia, the UK and Japan. Its Facebook pages, with around 560,000 followers, had likely been bought from spam operators, with followers mainly in Vietnam, Bangladesh and Brazil.3 Meta suggested the operators may simply have been trying to meet a production quota.

Size, in other words, is not impact. To compare operations in real time, Ben Nimmo, then at Graphika, proposed the Breakout Scale in September 2020. It sorts operations into six categories using only observable evidence:

  • Category 1: stays in one community on one platform.
  • Category 2: spreads across several platforms, or across several communities on one platform.
  • Category 3: spreads across several platforms and several communities.
  • Category 4: breaks out of social media and is amplified by mainstream media.
  • Category 5: is amplified by high-profile figures such as celebrities and political candidates.
  • Category 6: triggers a policy response or concrete action, or includes a call for violence.4

By that measure, presence on fifty platforms earns only a middling score. What pushes an operation up the scale is real audiences, journalists and public figures picking it up.

concepts.title: Who Gets Caught, and How
concepts.contentHtml:
Takedown reports can leave the impression that only Russia, China and Iran run influence operations. In August 2022 Graphika and the Stanford Internet Observatory corrected that. Twitter and Meta had removed two overlapping sets of accounts in July and August, and the researchers found an interconnected web on Twitter, Facebook, Instagram and five other platforms promoting pro-Western narratives in the Middle East and Central Asia over almost five years. The campaigns advanced the interests of the United States and its allies while opposing Russia, China and Iran. The report, "Unheard Voice", called it the most extensive case of covert pro-Western influence operations on social media reviewed by open-source researchers to date.1

The tactics were the standard kit: fake personas with GAN-generated faces, sham independent media outlets, memes, hashtag campaigns and petitions. So were the results. The vast majority of posts received no more than a handful of likes or retweets, and only 19% of the covert assets had more than 1,000 followers.2 Even well-resourced sponsors, it seems, fall back on a narrow repertoire.

Governments also act directly. On 4 September 2024 the US Justice Department announced the seizure of 32 internet domains used by Doppelganger, a campaign it said was run by the Russian companies Social Design Agency, Structura and ANO Dialog under the direction of the Russian Presidential Administration, in particular First Deputy Chief of Staff Sergei Kiriyenko.3 Doppelganger's signature was cybersquatting: registering look-alike domains such as washingtonpost.pm to publish Russian government messaging dressed as real news. Traffic came from influencers, paid social media adverts (some made with AI tools) and fake profiles posing as Americans. The legal hooks were not the propaganda itself but sanctions law, money laundering and criminal trademark violations, and the Treasury designated 10 individuals and two entities the same day.

Compare this with the IRA. A troll farm run by a private businessman has given way, at least in this case, to contractors directed from inside the Kremlin's administration, a reminder that actors adapt faster than the categories researchers use to describe them.

concepts.title: The Research Ecosystem Under Pressure
concepts.contentHtml:
The research in this topic depended on access: Twitter's archives, Meta's monitoring tools, data shared with the Senate. In 2024 much of that access shrank, and the field itself became a political target.

Tools. Meta shut down CrowdTangle, its tool for tracking public content on Facebook and Instagram, on 14 August 2024, less than three months before the US election, despite petitions from researchers to keep it running through January 2025.1 Its replacement, the Meta Content Library, requires researchers to apply and to come from qualified academic or nonprofit institutions. Brandi Geurkink of the Coalition for Independent Technology Research called CrowdTangle one of the best tools civil society had to monitor hate speech and election interference.

Institutions. The Stanford Internet Observatory ran the Election Integrity Partnership with the University of Washington to track false claims about the 2020 and 2022 elections. Republicans in Congress and the courts alleged that such work amounted to collusion to suppress conservative speech, a claim the researchers deny. After lawsuits, subpoenas and millions of dollars in legal fees, Stanford did not renew the contract of the observatory's research manager, Renée DiResta, in 2024, and the partnership said it would not work on the 2024 or future elections.2 Stanford insisted the observatory's work continued under new leadership. On 26 June 2024 the Supreme Court, in Murthy v. Missouri, ruled 6–3 that the states and individuals suing federal officials over pressure on platforms lacked standing, so it never reached the merits.3

Regulation. Europe moved the other way. On 2 July 2025 the European Commission published a delegated act under the Digital Services Act letting vetted researchers apply for the internal data of very large online platforms and search engines to study systemic risks in the EU, with the first researchers due to be vetted from October.4

Both sides of the American fight claim to defend free expression: one fears government-steered moderation, the other the chilling of academic inquiry. What nobody disputes is that whoever controls platform data controls what can be known about influence operations.

title: Generative AI and the Next Operations
description: What language models change for propagandists, what 2024 actually showed, and the open problems

concepts.title: What Language Models Change
concepts.contentHtml:
Running the IRA meant paying hundreds of people to write convincingly as Americans. Generative language models promise to automate exactly that labour. In January 2023 Josh Goldstein, Girish Sastry, Micah Musser, Renée DiResta, Matthew Gentzel and Katerina Sedova, from Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, OpenAI and the Stanford Internet Observatory, published a report assessing the threat. They organised it with the ABC framework from lesson 1: models could change who runs operations, how they behave and what they produce. They also mapped where defences could bite, at four stages: model construction, model access, content dissemination and belief formation.1 No single mitigation, they concluded, would fully prevent the threat, though a combination might make an important difference.

Could machine-written propaganda actually persuade? Goldstein, Jason Chao, Shelby Grossman, Alex Stamos and Michael Tomz tested it in a preregistered survey experiment with 8,221 US adults in December 2021, comparing real articles from covert foreign campaigns with text from GPT-3 davinci. Among people shown no article, 24.4% agreed with each propaganda thesis. Reading the original propaganda raised agreement to 47.4%; reading GPT-3's version raised it to 43.5%.2 With light human help, such as editing the prompt or picking the best of several outputs, the AI text matched or beat the originals. The authors concluded that propagandists could use AI to create convincing content with limited effort.3

Read these results precisely. They show that AI text can be as persuasive as human propaganda on a single reading, in a survey, on topics drawn from real campaigns. They do not show that AI helps operations reach more people, which is the bottleneck lesson 5 identified. The main change is in cost and fluency: a small team can now produce endless grammatical, varied text in any language, erasing tell-tale errors and making copy-paste fingerprints rarer.

concepts.title: The Record So Far
concepts.contentHtml:
2024 was billed as the year of the AI election, with more than 2 billion people expected at the polls. What actually happened is the best evidence yet, and it largely echoes the effects research of lesson 5.

In May 2024 OpenAI reported disrupting five covert operations that had used its models: Russia's Bad Grammar and Doppelganger, China's Spamouflage, an Iranian network called the International Union of Virtual Media, and an Israeli operation dubbed Zero Zeno. The models helped them generate text and images, in some cases with fewer language errors than human operators would have managed. Yet OpenAI found the operations did not appear to have benefited from meaningfully increased audience engagement or reach as a result.1 In December 2024 Meta reported that, across the year's major elections, ratings on AI content related to elections, politics and social topics represented less than 1% of all fact-checked misinformation.2 Its president of global affairs, Nick Clegg, judged any impact modest and limited in scope. Both are self-assessments by companies with an interest in the answer, but they match what independent researchers had predicted.

In October 2023 Felix Simon, Sacha Altay and Hugo Mercier argued that fears of an AI misinformation wave were overblown, because the consumption of misinformation is limited mostly by demand, not supply.3 Falsehood is already cheap and plentiful; more of it does not create more believers.

The clearest harm so far came from cloned audio, not text. Before New Hampshire's January 2024 primary, voters received robocalls in which an AI-generated voice resembling President Biden discouraged Democrats from voting. The political consultant behind them, Steve Kramer, faced a proposed US$6 million fine from the Federal Communications Commission and was indicted on 13 felony counts of voter suppression and 13 misdemeanour counts of impersonating a candidate.4 Notice what made it dangerous: it borrowed a trusted voice and reached voters directly by phone, skipping the platform bottleneck entirely.

concepts.title: Open Problems: Conversation and the Liar's Dividend
concepts.contentHtml:
The reassuring record of 2024 measured AI as a content factory feeding the old distribution system. The harder questions concern capabilities that system never had.

Persuasion by conversation. In December 2025 Kobi Hackenburg, Ben Tappin and colleagues from the Oxford Internet Institute, the UK AI Security Institute and other universities published the most comprehensive study to date, in Science: three experiments in which 76,977 UK adults discussed one of 707 political issues with one of 19 language models. Conversational AI was significantly more persuasive than static messages, and model size mattered only modestly. Post-training raised persuasiveness by up to 51% and prompting strategies by up to 27%, so small, widely available models could be tuned to match large proprietary ones.1 The most persuasive outputs were packed with fact-checkable claims, and there was a troubling trade-off: the more persuasive a model, the less accurate its information tended to be.2 The authors cautioned that real-world effects may be limited by how willing people are to hold long political conversations with a chatbot.

The liar's dividend. In 2019 the legal scholars Bobby Chesney and Danielle Citron warned of a subtler harm. As the public learns that video and audio can be faked, liars gain a defence: denounce authentic evidence as a deepfake. They called this the liar's dividend, and noted that it grows, perversely, in proportion to success in educating people about deepfakes. Every warning about synthetic media slightly devalues genuine evidence.

Measurement. Lessons 4 and 5 relied on fingerprints, coordination graphs and linked panel data. Fluent, varied AI text weakens text fingerprints; private chats and personalised dialogues leave no public trace to map; and platform data access, as lesson 6 showed, is contested. The frontier is therefore methodological: detecting operations whose content is unique, estimating the effects of persuasion that happens one conversation at a time, and keeping the evidence base independent of the companies being studied. The record so far counsels calm, but the IRA's story shows that operators adapt, and researchers have to adapt faster.
